title: Brightline SSO sign-in
summary: A link from an email opened a sign-in page that looks like your company SSO.

page.heading: Sign in to Brightline SSO
page.text: Your session has expired. Please re-enter your credentials to continue.

prompt: A link in an email opened this sign-in page. What do you do?

choices.label: Type my password and sign in
Check the address bar, then close the tab and go to the real portal myself
Enter a fake password to 'test' it first

red_flags.title: Lookalike address
red_flags.explanation: The real portal is on your corporate domain. This page is on secure-login.example with your company name only as a prefix, a classic lookalike.

what_to_do: Never sign in through a link in an email or message. Open your bookmark or type the known address yourself.
Read the full domain in the address bar, right to left; the real site is the part just before the first single slash.
If you already entered a password, change it now and report it; attackers use stolen credentials within minutes.
lesson: A padlock and a familiar logo prove nothing. Only the domain in the address bar tells you where you really are.

title: "Verify you are human"
summary: A page claims you must complete a verification step by pasting something into your computer.

page.heading: Verify you are human
page.text: To confirm you are not a robot, complete the quick verification below.
steps: Press Ctrl + V to paste the verification code

prompt: The page wants you to copy a 'verification code' and run it. What do you do?

choices.label: Follow the steps and paste the code
Close the page — a real check never asks me to run commands
Copy the code but don't run it, just to look

red_flags.title: It tells you to run something
red_flags.explanation: No genuine CAPTCHA asks you to open the Run box, a terminal, or File Explorer and paste anything. That sequence runs an attacker's command on your machine.

what_to_do: Never paste anything a web page tells you to into the Run box, PowerShell, a terminal, or File Explorer.
Close the tab. If you pasted and ran it, disconnect from the network and tell IT immediately.
Remember the shape of this trick ("ClickFix"): a fake error or CAPTCHA plus copy-paste instructions.
lesson: A website can put text on your clipboard, but only you can run it. The whole scam depends on you pasting it somewhere dangerous.

title: App permission request
summary: An app is asking for permission to your mailbox and files. The sign-in page itself is genuine.

permissions: Read, send, and permanently delete your email
Read all files you have access to
Maintain access to data you have given it access to

prompt: You clicked a link and a real sign-in now asks you to grant this app access. What do you do?

choices.label: Click Accept so I can use the app
Deny — an unverified app does not need my whole mailbox
Accept for now and remove it later

red_flags.title: Unverified publisher
red_flags.explanation: A legitimate business app is almost always from a verified publisher. 'Unverified' on a permissions screen is a serious warning.

red_flags.title: Excessive permissions
red_flags.explanation: Reading, sending and deleting all your mail and files is far more than a small helper app needs. Granting it hands an attacker your account without ever stealing a password.

what_to_do: Deny access and close the page. Only approve app permissions you expected and that match what the app does.
Consent phishing skips your password and MFA entirely, so the sign-in looking genuine is not reassurance.
Report it; your IT team can block the app for everyone and check who else approved it.
lesson: Consent phishing asks for access, not your password. The login can be real and the trap still springs when you click Accept.

title: "Your browser is out of date"
summary: A full-page banner says your browser is dangerously out of date and offers a download.

page.heading: Your browser is out of date
page.text: You are missing critical security updates. Download the latest version now to stay protected.

prompt: A website is telling you to download a browser update. What do you do?

choices.label: Ignore it — real updates come from the browser, not a web page
Download it but scan it before running

red_flags.title: A web page cannot update your browser
red_flags.explanation: Browsers update themselves in the background or through their own settings. Any site offering a browser 'update' download is serving malware.

what_to_do: Close the tab. Check for genuine updates only inside the browser's own menu (for example, Help or Settings, then About).
Do not run installers offered by a random website, even if the page looks urgent or official.
If you downloaded and ran it, treat the device as compromised and contact IT.
lesson: Software updates come from the software itself, never from a web page telling you that you are at risk.
